study_identification.title: Neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia revisited: similarity in individual deviation and idiosyncrasy from the normative model of whole-brain white matter tracts and shared brain-cognition covariation with ADHD and ASD

study_characteristics.study_objective: To investigate the similarity and differences in white matter (WM) tract deviations from normative ranges among schizophrenia (at different illness stages), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and to examine whether linked dimensions of cognition and brain metrics cut across diagnostic boundaries per the Research Domain Criteria framework.

dataset_name.answer: Single-site dataset from National Taiwan University Hospital and community recruitment

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Diffusion spectrum imaging protocol with 102 diffusion-encoding directions with maximal b value of 4000 s/mm2; single-shot spin-echo echo-planar imaging sequence with twice-refocused diffusion-sensitive gradients; mean-apparent propagator models for GFA computation; deterministic streamline-based tractography; diffeomorphic registration for spatial normalization; 45 major WM tracts extracted based on DSI template

quality_checking_detail.answer: Rigorous quality control by excluding participants with low signal-noise ratio (SNR) or high signal-dropout counts (SDC), a proxy of in-scanner motion levels. SNR and SDC were comparable between groups. The derived Z-scores of clinical groups and TDC were not correlated with age, SNR, or in-scanner motion levels.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Single-site study from the same 3-Tesla Siemens TIM Trio scanner with a 32-channel phased-array head coil at National Taiwan University Hospital. All participants received MRI scans on the same scanner, eliminating site/scanner effects.

modeling_method.answer: Moving average approach for age-specific normative modeling

response_variable.answer: Generalized fractional anisotropy (GFA) of 45 major white matter tracts

predictor_effects.answer: Sex-specific normative age models were constructed. Moving average approach was used to obtain unbiased mean and variance estimates for the GFA metric in each age range. Models were stratified by sex.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some nuisance structures through quality control (SNR, signal dropout, in-scanner motion) and confirms that derived Z-scores are not correlated with these metrics. However, the normative model validation itself in terms of handling nuisance structure is not extensively described. The moving average approach is used for modeling, but comprehensive validation metrics (e.g., explained variance, MSLL, skewness, kurtosis of residuals) are not reported.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: The rigorous quality control of MRI data was implemented by excluding those with low signal-noise ratio (SNR) or high signal-dropout counts (SDC), a proxy of in-scanner motion levels. As a result, SNR and SDC were comparable between these groups... The derived Z-scores of clinical groups and TDC were not correlated with age, SNR, or in-scanner motion levels (SFig. 1).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The paper does not report validation using same-domain non-independent data (e.g., holdout validation, cross-validation within the training dataset). The normative model was built on 626 typically developing controls and directly applied to clinical groups without reported internal validation procedures.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Individualized tract-deviation profiles comprised GFA Z-scores of each WM tract derived from the sex-specific normative age models, constructed from 626 TDCs (Male/Female: 376/250; age range 5-40, 20.16 ± 8.5 yrs). A moving average approach was used to obtain the unbiased mean and variance estimates for the GFA metric in each age range.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study does not report validation using an independent typically developing cohort from the same domain. All 626 TDCs were used to construct the normative model, and no separate independent validation cohort of healthy controls is mentioned.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Individualized tract-deviation profiles comprised GFA Z-scores of each WM tract derived from the sex-specific normative age models, constructed from 626 TDCs (Male/Female: 376/250; age range 5-40, 20.16 ± 8.5 yrs).

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study does not report validation of the normative model using a different domain dataset (e.g., external cohort from a different site, scanner, or country). The entire study is single-site based on the same scanner.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Participants received MRI scans on the same 3-Tesla Siemens TIM Trio scanner with a 32-channel phased-array head coil. The diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) protocol was detailed elsewhere.

clinical_dataset.answer: Single-site dataset from National Taiwan University Hospital Department of Psychiatry

diseases_studied.answer: Schizophrenia (SCZ); Autism spectrum disorder (ASD); Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)

clinical_groups_age.answer: Schizophrenia overall: 25.8±5.8 years (16-40 years); First-episode: 20.2±8.5 years; Subchronic and Chronic ages available in STable 1; ASD: 16.35±4.2 years (9-35 years); ADHD: 18.20±8.6 years (7-38 years)

clinical_groups_sex.answer: Schizophrenia: sex distribution in Table 1; ASD: M158 (90.3%) F17 (9.7%); ADHD: M206 (73.8%) F75 (26.2%)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score derived from sex-specific normative age models; Effect size (Cohen's d) of one-sample t-test on GFA Z-scores for each WM tract indicating deviation extent from the norm; F-ratio (tract GFA Z-score variance of a subgroup divided by tract variance of TDC norm) from F-test for idiosyncrasy metric

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Two-sample t-tests for between-group deviation comparisons; F-tests for between-group idiosyncrasy comparisons; Spearman's correlation (ρ) of WM tract deviation and idiosyncrasy profiles between groups; Propensity score weights matching for age; False-discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons across 45 WM tracts; Unsupervised machine learning (Ward's hierarchical clustering and k-means clustering) using principal component analysis on GFA Z-scores; Gap statistics for optimal cluster number; Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) separately for CANTAB and IQ measures to identify linked dimensions of cognition and WM deviations; 100,000 permutations for FWE-corrected significance testing in CCA
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Schizophrenia, particularly at earlier stages, showed similar patterns of WM deviation and idiosyncrasy to ASD and ADHD, with similarity decreasing as schizophrenia progressed to chronic stages; unsupervised machine learning could not separate schizophrenia from neurodevelopmental disorders based on WM deviation patterns; a shared linked dimension of cognition and WM deviations was identified across all three disorders.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Patients with schizophrenia showed widespread significantly negative deviations in most major WM tracts, with chronic schizophrenia showing more pronounced deviations (maximum Cohen's d: -0.93 in chronic vs. -0.72 in first-episode or -0.79 in subchronic) and greater numbers of altered tracts (18 tracts in chronic, 11 in first-episode, 6 in subchronic with Cohen's d < -0.5). Significant correlations in deviation patterns were found between first-episode schizophrenia and ASD (ρ=0.462, p=0.001) and ADHD (ρ=0.296, p=0.048), and between subchronic schizophrenia and ASD (ρ=0.326, p=0.029) and ADHD (ρ=0.580, p<0.001), but not between chronic schizophrenia and either ASD or ADHD. Schizophrenia showed more negative deviations than neurodevelopmental disorders in bilateral fornix (-1.04≤Cohen's d≤-0.71), uncinate fasciculus (-0.74≤Cohen's d≤-0.42), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi (-0.81≤Cohen's d≤-0.38), inferior longitudinal fasciculus (-0.99≤Cohen's d≤-0.40), thalamic radiations (-0.83≤Cohen's d≤-0.24), and frontostriatal tracts (-0.65≤Cohen's d≤-0.22). Unsupervised machine learning (Gap statistics) indicated optimal cluster number of 1, suggesting schizophrenia cannot be differentiated from ADHD and ASD using WM tract deviation profiles. Canonical correlation analysis identified one significant dimension (r=0.59, pFWE=0.036) linking working memory with deviations in fornix, uncinate fasciculi, IFOF, and ILF across all three disorders.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Unknown effects of psychotropic medications on findings; number of psychotic relapses may influence brain structures beyond illness duration; some ADHD/ASD children were under common age of schizophrenia onset (though none showed psychotic symptoms); participants with intellectual disabilities were excluded, limiting certain angles of inference
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study provides novel evidence supporting the neurodevelopmental model of schizophrenia, demonstrating that schizophrenia lies on a neurodevelopmental continuum. The findings suggest that whole-brain WM microstructural composition in earlier stages of schizophrenia is closer to that of neurodevelopmental disorders. The similarity in WM deviation patterns and shared cognitive dimensions across schizophrenia, ASD, and ADHD support conceptualizing schizophrenia as a neurodevelopmental condition. However, specific fiber bundles (thalamic radiations, frontostriatal, hippocampal connections, long association fibers) are selectively unique in schizophrenia, particularly at later stages, suggesting distinct neural correlates that separate schizophrenia from typical neurodevelopmental disorders.

general_notes.general_notes: This is a single-site study conducted at National Taiwan University Hospital using a harmonized imaging protocol on the same scanner, which eliminates site/scanner effects but may limit generalizability. The study employed duration-based staging of schizophrenia (first-episode <1 year, subchronic 1-10 years, chronic ≥10 years) with different chlorpromazine equivalent doses across stages (first-episode: 211.0±223.6 mg/d; subchronic: 268.6±231.8 mg/d; chronic: 370.6±256.1 mg/d). All participants had full-scale IQ >70. None of the ASD or ADHD participants had co-occurring psychotic disorders, and none of the schizophrenia participants had childhood diagnoses of ASD or ADHD. The study utilized diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) rather than conventional diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), with GFA as the primary WM metric, though supplementary analyses with DTI-derived metrics (axial diffusivity, radial diffusivity, mean diffusivity) largely replicated the GFA findings. The normative modeling approach used moving averages for age-specific estimation, which differs from more commonly used regression-based approaches (e.g., GPR, GAMLSS). Age-matching analyses using propensity score weights were performed to address age differences between groups. The study is notable for its focus on individual-level deviations rather than group-average approaches, and for examining both deviation magnitude and inter-individual variability (idiosyncrasy) across different illness stages of schizophrenia.
